The "Magnificent Seven" is a grouping of stocks used to describe some of the largest companies in the world that have helped lead the U.S. stock market higher over the past decade. It is made up of:

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL)

Nvidia

Microsoft

Alphabet

Amazon

Meta Platforms

Tesla

For U.S.-listed stocks, all seven of these are in the top 10, so being on this list is a big deal. However, 2026 hasn't been the greatest year for the Magnificent Seven. The S&P 500 is up about 12.3% this year, and only three stocks are outperforming it: Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft. But which one of these is doing the best? It's the non-AI one.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Apple leads all Magnificent Seven stocks

The top performer so far in 2026 has been Apple, up about 29%. That's practically double the second-best performer, Amazon, which has risen around 15%. So, what has separated Apple from the competition? I think there are two reasons.

First, Apple really isn't an AI stock. While its products have some AI features, it's not spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers like every other company on this list (besides Nvidia, which is selling the equipment for these data centers). As a whole, the market has been a bit bearish on the AI buildout lately, and Apple has been a haven for investors who aren't as keen on the long-term prospects of AI.

In fact, Apple is the only stock among the top 10 largest companies on U.S. exchanges that doesn't have significant AI investments or business cases riding on the AI buildout. This has made it a safe haven for non-AI investors and has boosted its stock.

Another reason Apple has done well this year is that its iPhone 17 lineup was the most popular of any of its previous models. This has driven sales growth and has made Apple a respectable business again.

However, Apple's day of reckoning could be coming. Outside of Tesla (which has a sky-high valuation of 424 times trailing earnings), Apple is by far the most expensive stock in the Magnificent Seven.

NVDA PE Ratio data by YCharts

As a result, I think the stock could be getting a bit too pricey, and investors need to watch out. Apple's strong performance this year hasn't come entirely from business results, and if the market flips its stance on AI and becomes bullish on it again, Apple's stock could sell off in favor of some AI-focused investments. It's about as good as it gets for Apple sentiment right now. As a result, I don't think Apple stock is a buy right now.

title: Tesla's FSD (Supervised) Attach Rate Hit 75% on New Vehicles. Here's Why That Single Number Could Matter More Than Robotaxi for the Stock in 2027.
detail:
Tesla's FSD (Supervised) Attach Rate Hit 75% on New Vehicles. Here's Why That Single Number Could Matter More Than Robotaxi for the Stock in 2027.
Jeff Siegel, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 9:10 AM CST 4 min read
TSLA
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) reported that more than 75% of its new vehicle deliveries in North America included a paid Full Self-Driving (Supervised) subscription sign-up in the third quarter of 2026. That's an increase of nearly 20 percentage points from the previous quarter's attach rate.

For a company spending billions developing autonomous vehicles, artificial intelligence, and humanoid robots, this might be one of the most encouraging numbers in its latest earnings report. And unlike the robotaxi, FSD (Supervised) is already generating revenue from customers driving vehicles they own.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Tesla's software business is gaining traction

Tesla ended the third quarter with approximately 1.74 million active paid FSD customers worldwide, up from 1.48 million in the second quarter and 1.04 million a year earlier. That's roughly 67% annual growth.

Tesla also reported that about half of its paid FSD customers were using subscriptions rather than paying up front. Those subscribers generate revenue month after month, potentially creating a predictable software business alongside Tesla's automotive operations.

Consider this hypothetical scenario: If Tesla eventually reaches 2 million paying monthly subscribers at $99 per month, that would translate into approximately $2.38 billion in annualized subscription revenue. At 3 million subscribers, the figure jumps to $3.56 billion.

These aren't Tesla's revenue forecasts. They illustrate what a larger subscription business could generate, assuming customers keep paying throughout the year. And software revenue could carry attractive margins because Tesla doesn't have to manufacture another vehicle every time someone subscribes.

Image source: Getty Images.
There's still a catch with that 75% figure

Tesla's reported attach rate measures sign-ups at delivery. It doesn't tell investors how many customers continue paying after the initial period. In fact, management acknowledged during its earnings call that new vehicles come with a free FSD trial and that the company isn't yet providing detailed customer retention or cancellation rates.

Yes, a 75% sign-up rate is impressive, but a 75% long-term retention rate for paying customers would be far more valuable. FSD also remains a supervised driver-assistance system and is not to be seen as autonomous. Drivers must pay attention and be prepared to intervene. It isn't the same as the fully autonomous service Tesla hopes to expand through its robotaxi business. That said, there's been no indication that supervised FSD has presented much of an obstacle for customers who have opted for the subscription.

Ryan Vanzo, The Motley Fool

Trading disclosure

Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) CEO Elon Musk formally unveiled the Cybertruck in 2019. Actual production didn't begin until 2024. Next year, production will formally end, according to a new tweet from Musk.

Musk shared on social media that the electric vehicle (EV) maker will wind down "production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year."

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Why is the Cybertruck going extinct? Slow sales are largely to blame. According to estimates, Tesla is only selling a few thousand units per quarter. If the Cybertruck were a mass success like the Model 3 and Model Y, it likely would not be getting the axe.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk. Image source: The White House.

But there's another obvious reason that Tesla is winding down production for one of its least successful models ever.

Here's why Tesla is ending Cybertruck production

Tesla's $1.4 trillion valuation isn't based on its success as an automaker. Instead, the market is pricing in plenty of growth for other opportunities, namely AI, humanoid robots, and self-driving cars. All of these initiatives will be capital-intensive to scale. Freeing up capital by ending a low-volume, low-potential model is a wise decision for Tesla as it pivots its priorities toward the future.

Just as importantly, Tesla will then be able to use the factory space to focus on Cybercab production. Musk said so directly, tweeting that ceasing Cybertruck production is designed specifically "to make room for increased Cybercab production."

Some experts believe that the robotaxi market will eventually be valued at $8 trillion to $10 trillion globally. Success in that market can move the needle for Tesla in a way Cybertruck demand never could.

title: Tesla Stock Hasn't Closed at a Record in Nearly 11 Months. Here's How Its Past Record Droughts Ended.
detail:
Tesla Stock Hasn't Closed at a Record in Nearly 11 Months. Here's How Its Past Record Droughts Ended.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 5:37 AM CST 5 min read
TSLA
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) last closed at a record on Dec. 16, 2025, at $489.88 a share. That was 327 days ago, or nearly 11 months. With Tesla shares trading near $346 as I write this, the stock would have to gain about 41% just to tie it.

Long gaps between records are nothing new for the EV maker, though. Since its IPO in June 2010, Tesla stock has gone 300 days or more without a record close six other times, based on daily split-adjusted closing prices.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Every one of those droughts eventually ended. But what happened next was very different. Two of them gave way to rallies of over 600%. The other four were followed by a new drought within months, and twice within days.

And the difference between the two groups probably boils down to whether Tesla's profits were turning higher.

Image source: Getty Images.

Long waits are common for Tesla

The first two droughts came early in the electric-vehicle maker's life as a public company. The stock spent 474 days without a record from Nov. 24, 2010, to March 12, 2012, and then exactly 300 days from April 3, 2012, to Jan. 28, 2013. The next two lasted longer, at 942 days from Sept. 4, 2014, to April 3, 2017, and 821 days from Sept. 18, 2017, to Dec. 18, 2019. Most recently, shares went 1,133 days from Nov. 4, 2021, to Dec. 11, 2024, and then 364 days from Dec. 17, 2024, to last December's record.

That makes the current 327-day wait the second shortest of the seven. The middle of the six past droughts is around 650 days, or almost twice as long as this one has lasted.

Of course, the drops along the way were steep. In the 2021-to-2024 drought, the stock's lowest close was around 74% below its prior record.

And in every one of the six, shares closed at least 31% under the old high at some point. This time, the low so far was $298.32 on July 29, around 39% below the December record.

What happened when the droughts ended?

Two of them ended in huge runs. Once the 300-day gap closed on Jan. 28, 2013, Tesla stock kept setting records until Sept. 4, 2014, rising around 652% in that time.

And once the drought ended on Dec. 18, 2019, shares climbed about 1,464% to the November 2021 record that started the longest wait of all.

The other four runs were short. The March 2012 record led to just 22 days of new highs before the next drought began. The April 2017 record brought around five and a half months of records and a 29% climb.

detail:
Elon Musk Is Winding Down Cybertruck Production to Build Cybercabs. The Model S and Model X Already Gave Up Their Factory Space to Robots.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 4:01 PM CST 5 min read
TSLA
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X on Friday that the company will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory around the middle of next year. The goal is to make room for more Cybercabs, Tesla's two-seat robotaxi. Musk didn't say if Tesla would build the truck somewhere else.

The Cybertruck isn't the first vehicle to give up its place this year. In January, Musk said Tesla would stop production of the Model S and Model X. The company has since replaced those lines at its Fremont, California, plant with production of its Optimus humanoid robot.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

At first glance, this is a big shake-up of Tesla's lineup. Measured by sales, though, it isn't.

Vehicles other than the Model 3 and Model Y (mostly the Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck) made up about 3% of the EV maker's 1.64 million deliveries in 2025.

Measured by factory space, the change is much bigger. And I think the gap between those two measures matters more for the stock than for the car business.

Image source: Getty Images.

Lines built for far more

Showing how much room these three vehicles took up, Tesla's installed-capacity table at the end of 2025 rated its Model S and Model X line at 100,000 vehicles a year and its Cybertruck line at over 125,000. Combined, they could build more than 225,000 vehicles yearly, or almost 10% of the more than 2.35 million vehicles Tesla's car plants were rated for.

But Tesla made just 53,900 vehicles outside the Model 3 and Model Y in all of 2025 -- under a quarter of what those lines were built for. And deliveries in this group dropped 40% from 2024, to 50,850.

The slide kept going in 2026. Other-model deliveries fell from 16,130 in the first quarter (probably boosted by final orders for the S and X) to 12,364 in the second quarter and 8,295 in the third. The third-quarter total was down 48% year over year.

The Cybertruck, of course, never got close to filling its line. Tesla doesn't break out sales by model, but Cox Automotive estimated U.S. Cybertruck sales at around 20,000 in 2025, down from about 39,000 in 2024. Musk once said the truck would one day sell 250,000 a year.

Put another way, even if the Cybertruck goes away forever, Tesla is giving up very little to free up this space. Tesla's automotive sales revenue fell just 1% year over year in the third quarter. And its quarterly filing linked slightly lower deliveries mostly to fewer Model S and Model X sales.

detail:
Every Humanoid Robot Needs Rare-Earth Magnets. Here's the American Stock Positioned to Sell Them -- and It's Down 62%.

The rise of humanoid robots could be one of the next decade's most important technology trends. Tesla is betting heavily on its Optimus robots and expects humanoid robotics to become its most important product category. Meanwhile, Chinese pure plays including Unitree Robotics are also aiming to build leading positions in the fledgling tech category.

Rising demand for humanoid robots is set to push demand for rare-earth minerals and magnets even higher because these elements and composites are crucial foundations for some of the capabilities that make these robots special. There's a catch, though. Geopolitical dynamics and broader supply constraints mean that sourcing rare-earth materials and magnets could be very difficult -- especially for U.S.-based companies.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The good news is that MP Materials (NYSE: MP) is positioning itself to address this potentially huge supply chain issue, and it could wind up delivering big wins for patient investors.

Image source: Getty Images.
Rare-earth materials have become a crucial supply chain variable

While the U.S. and China maintain formal diplomatic relations, it's no secret that the two countries are the foremost competing world powers and are taking steps to gain an edge over each other. Along those lines, China's control over the extraction, refinement, and production of usable rare-earth minerals and magnets is a strength that the country is leveraging against the U.S. and its allies.

According to some estimates, China is responsible for roughly 60% of global rare-earth mining and 90% of processing. China is already using its stranglehold on the rare-earth market as a trade and geopolitical bargaining chip, and it could completely block exports if relations with the U.S. worsen. That could deal a crushing blow to U.S.-based manufacturers of humanoid robots.

According to MP Materials CEO James Litinsky, each humanoid robot will need between 8 and 10 pounds of rare-earth-magnet content in order to facilitate movement across various articulated joints. On a comparative basis, this works out to between double and triple the amount found in electric vehicles.

Litinsky believes that humanoid robots will become a major economic and defense sector resource for the U.S., and that means that his company could be poised to enjoy surging demand and pricing power. Meanwhile, the company's share price is down roughly 62% from its high amid concerns about whether the company's growth bets will come to fruition and doubts about just how much pricing power MP will actually be able to command in the rare-earth magnets space.
